entries.knownHazards: The plant contains calcium oxylate crystals. These cause an extremely unpleasant sensation similar to needles being stuck into the mouth and tongue if they are eaten, but they are easily neutralized by thoroughly drying or cooking the plant or by steeping it in water[65].

entries.flagReason: FACT FIDELITY: EN describes sensation as 'similar to needles being stuck into the mouth and tongue' — a sharp pricking/piercing character. LT renders this as 'stiprų deginimo pojūtį' (strong burning sensation), which shifts the character from needle-prick to burning heat. These are distinct sensations; calcium oxalate is known for mechanical irritation (raphide needle crystals), not heat.
entries.suggestedFix: Replace 'stiprų deginimo pojūtį' with 'aštrų duriantį pojūtį' (sharp pricking sensation) to preserve the needle-prick character described in EN.

entries.knownHazards: Although we have found no reports of toxicity for this species, a number of ferns contain carcinogens so some caution is advisable[200]. Many ferns also contain thiaminase, an enzyme that robs the body of its vitamin B complex. In small quantities this enzyme will do no harm to people eating an adequate diet that is rich in vitamin B, though large quantities can cause severe health problems. The enzyme is destroyed by heat or thorough drying, so cooking the plant will remove the thiaminase[172].
